scope: Scene-local provider measurements for canvas cue regressions. The intro uses the current course narrator. Other scenes retain their original measured windows.

beats.say: Draw independent standard-normal noise. Scale this fixed noise by the standard deviation, then add the mean. The resulting point is a posterior sample. The randomness entered through the noise; the transformation is differentiable in the encoder's outputs.

visual_cues.phrase: Scale this fixed noise by the standard deviation
then add the mean

beats.say: Keep the noise fixed and move the mean. The sample follows by the same amount. Change the scale and the fixed noise sets that movement. These derivatives let reconstruction gradients reach the encoder. That is reparameterization.

visual_cues.phrase: move the mean
Change the scale

beats.say: For generation, draw directly from the prior. Our fixed prior draw goes into the same hand-built decoder. Watch that exact point produce the displayed pattern. In a trained VAE, we inspect many prior draws to see whether this sampling route produces useful pictures.

visual_cues.phrase: Our fixed prior draw
Watch that exact point produce the displayed pattern

beats.say: Four pixels make up this badge. Flag any pixel brighter than point nine. Which corner gets a flag?

visual_cues.phrase: Four pixels make up this badge
brighter than point nine

beats.say: The bottom right. The bottom left sits exactly on the line. Keep your eye on those two corners as we pack this crop into two numbers.

visual_cues.phrase: The bottom right

beats.say: Our hand-built encoder takes the average of the four badge pixels. Its second number averages the two pixels just below them. This pair is the latent code. The decoder has to rebuild the picture from that pair. Together these two maps form an autoencoder. Will the rebuilt badge still tell us which corner to flag?

visual_cues.phrase: takes the average of the four badge pixels
averages the two pixels just below them
This pair is the latent code

beats.say: Brightness runs from zero to one. Our first coordinate watches these four center pixels. Add their brightness values, then divide the sum by four. That average is the first dial. A learned encoder would discover its own weights across many crops.

visual_cues.phrase: Add their brightness values
divide the sum by four

beats.say: The second dial averages these two lower pixels. Add them and divide by two. Now the decoder receives this pair. Its weights turn the regional brightness values into the reconstructed badge. The code is the only path carrying information about this particular input.

visual_cues.phrase: Add them and divide by two
turn the regional brightness values into the reconstructed badge

beats.say: Exchange the brightest and dimmest selected center pixels. We have changed their arrangement. Predict the new code before I uncover it. Will either dial change?

visual_cues.phrase: Exchange the brightest and dimmest selected center pixels
Predict the new code

beats.say: The pair stays the same. The sum is unchanged, so both averages survive the exchange. The decoder therefore produces the same reconstruction for two different inputs. We have found a precise detail that this bottleneck loses.

visual_cues.phrase: The pair stays the same
produces the same reconstruction

beats.say: Let's measure that reconstruction. Select the same pixel in both grids. Subtract its decoded value from its input value. Then square the difference. Opposite signs now contribute positive errors, and larger misses receive a larger penalty.

visual_cues.phrase: Subtract its decoded value from its input value
square the difference

beats.say: Repeat this for every pixel and add the squared errors. Finally, divide the total by twenty-five. That is mean squared error, or MSE. Training adjusts both functions to reduce it. This score describes our one reconstruction; let's also test what changing the code actually does.

visual_cues.phrase: Repeat this for every pixel and add the squared errors
divide the total by twenty-five

beats.say: Here is a second constructed crop with its brightness lower down. Our encoder gives it a different pair. Keep the original badge on the left, and replace its code with this lower-region code. Predict where the decoder will put the bright region.

visual_cues.phrase: second constructed crop with its brightness lower down
replace its code with this lower-region code

beats.say: The output moves downward, and its error against the original badge rises. The decoder uses the message we send. Plain reconstruction training evaluates the codes reached by training inputs. A random draw asks it to work elsewhere too. A VAE connects those jobs by defining a distribution over codes.

visual_cues.phrase: The output moves downward
error against the original badge rises

beats.say: A variational autoencoder begins with a generative model: draw a code from a prior, then draw a picture from the decoder distribution. Given an observed crop, its encoder selects an approximate posterior: a distribution of possible codes for that crop. Here we use supplied Gaussian parameters.

visual_cues.phrase: encoder selects an approximate posterior

beats.say: Change the input to the lower crop. Its mean moves, while the gray standard-normal prior stays fixed at zero with unit variance. Our diagonal Gaussian treats its coordinates as independent for this input.

visual_cues.phrase: Change the input to the lower crop. Its mean moves

beats.say: Return to the badge and start the first width at one. The encoder predicts log variance. Halve that value and exponentiate to get standard deviation. Watch the first axis narrow. This positive standard deviation is the scale we will use to sample.

visual_cues.phrase: Return to the badge and start the first width at one
Halve that value and exponentiate to get standard deviation

beats.say: Reconstruction asks the code to preserve the crop. Kullback-Leibler divergence, or KL, penalizes posterior mismatch from the prior. Match the means and variances and KL is zero. Move them away and the penalty grows. Its closed form sums the contributions from our two latent coordinates.

visual_cues.phrase: Move them away and the penalty grows

beats.say: Hold reconstruction fixed. Increase the KL coefficient and its contribution grows. During training, both terms can change. Log them separately so you can see the compromise.

visual_cues.phrase: Increase the KL coefficient

beats.say: Our mean error divides the squared-error sum by the pixel count. For a Gaussian pixel likelihood, use the summed error divided by twice the observation variance, plus its constant. With coefficient one and that negative log likelihood, the objective is the negative evidence lower bound. Declare these reductions when defining the model.

visual_cues.phrase: mean error divides the squared-error sum by the pixel count
summed error divided by twice the observation variance
With coefficient one and that negative log likelihood

beats.say: These two fixed probes produce different pictures. Now reduce the decoder's code sensitivity to zero while the posteriors approach the prior. The outputs converge to their average in this deterministic squared-error toy. Losing input-specific latent information this way is posterior collapse.

visual_cues.phrase: reduce the decoder's code sensitivity to zero

beats.say: Swap the codes again. The pictures stay identical. Low KL and this insensitivity together warn of collapse. A richer decoder can produce varied pictures while still ignoring its global code.

visual_cues.phrase: Swap the codes again

beats.say: A vector-quantized autoencoder gives the decoder a learned codebook entry. The encoder proposes a vector. Compare the three squared distances, then send the nearest entry to the decoder. A learned prior over code combinations supplies useful discrete samples after training.

visual_cues.phrase: Compare the three squared distances
send the nearest entry to the decoder

beats.say: Nearest-entry assignment is piecewise constant. Reconstruction uses an approximate straight-through path to the encoder, and trains the decoder. The codebook loss moves the selected entry toward the proposal. Commitment pulls the proposal toward its entry. Follow these separate gradients from the same forward values. The other entries stay fixed.

visual_cues.phrase: Reconstruction uses an approximate straight-through path to the encoder, and trains the decoder
codebook loss moves the selected entry toward the proposal
Commitment pulls the proposal toward its entry

beats.say: At stride eight, each 8 by 8 input tile corresponds to one position in the spatial latent grid. So 512 by 512 becomes 64 by 64: 64 times fewer positions. Channel width and precision still affect cost. Our opening badge asks the final question: which detail did that compact code preserve?

visual_cues.phrase: At stride eight, each 8 by 8 input tile corresponds to one position in the spatial latent grid
64 times fewer positions
Channel width and precision

changed.previousSay: This screenshot records brightness from zero to one. Look at the four pixels in the badge. Suppose we flag a pixel only when its brightness is above point nine. Which corner would you flag?
